This manual follows Steps 1–6 of Supplement S2.4, “Computation of the MEC-Cox Estimator via the Dual Newton Solver,” in the same order and with the same notation. Each step retains the supplement’s derivation and is followed by the corresponding R code. The default example uses the package’s simulated data, logistic regression for source propensity, Cox regression for control survival, and the Kullback–Leibler (KL) generator. Steps 1 and 2 also provide executable RSF and machine-learning alternatives. The general generator notation from the supplement is retained.

R Markdown source · Package repository

1. Data and notation

1-1. Problem setting

We combine a treated target cohort with an external-control cohort, such as controls from a historical trial or another data source. For subject ii, the indicator Ai=1A_i=1 identifies a treated-cohort member receiving the treatment of interest, whereas Ai=0A_i=0 identifies an external-control member receiving control. Source membership and treatment status therefore coincide in this setting. The two cohorts can differ in their baseline covariates XiX_i, including characteristics that predict survival.

Let TiaT_i^a be the potential event time under treatment regime aa, with a=1a=1 denoting treatment and a=0a=0 denoting control. The target comparison is between Ti1∣Ai=1T_i^1\mid A_i=1 and Ti0∣Ai=1T_i^0\mid A_i=1: the survival experience of the treated target population under each regime. For a treated subject, the control potential event time is unobserved. External controls contribute information about control survival through their observed follow-up. With TiT_i denoting the event time under the treatment actually received and CiC_i the censoring time, each subject contributes Yi=min⁡(Ti,Ci)Y_i=\min(T_i,C_i) and δi=I(Ti≤Ci)\delta_i=I(T_i\le C_i).

Write S1a(t)=Pr⁡(Tia>t∣Ai=1)S_1^a(t)=\Pr(T_i^a>t\mid A_i=1) for marginal survival under regime aa in the treated target population, and let λ1a(t)\lambda_1^a(t) be the corresponding marginal hazard. The subscript 11 identifies the target population; the superscript aa identifies the treatment regime. Under the paper’s marginal proportional hazards model, λ1a(t)=λ10(t)exp⁡(θATTa),a=0,1, \lambda_1^a(t)=\lambda_1^0(t)\exp(\theta_{ATT}a), \qquad a=0,1, the parameter of interest is the ATT marginal hazard ratio HRATT=λ11(t)λ10(t)=exp⁡(θATT). HR_{ATT}=\frac{\lambda_1^1(t)}{\lambda_1^0(t)} =\exp(\theta_{ATT}). Both hazards refer to the treated target population. Under the inverse-probability-weighted Cox regression framework, MEC-Cox estimates this comparison by retaining treated subjects with weight one and calibrating the analysis weights of the external controls.

Figure 1 shows the treated-population comparison and how cross-fitted propensity scores and control-survival features enter the MEC-Cox weighting and estimation steps.

The source propensity score π(Xi)=Pr⁡(Ai=1∣Xi)\pi(X_i)=\Pr(A_i=1\mid X_i) describes how cohort membership varies with measured covariates. Its estimated odds provide the normalized baseline ATT weights d̂i\widehat d_i for external controls. MEC-Cox then updates these weights to ŵi\widehat w_i so that selected cross-fitted control-survival features ĥi\widehat h_i have the same totals in the weighted external controls and the treated cohort. The treated total is TH=∑i∈ℐ1ĥiT_H=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_1}\widehat h_i, where ℐa={i:Ai=a}\mathcal I_a=\{i:A_i=a\}. Steps 1–5 below construct these quantities and solve the calibration problem; Step 6 fits the final weighted Cox model and reports HR̂MEC=exp⁡(θ̂MEC)\widehat{HR}_{\mathrm{MEC}}=\exp(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MEC}}). The learner’s S0(t∣Xi)S_0(t\mid X_i) in Step 1 is conditional control survival; S1a(t)S_1^a(t) above is marginal survival in the treated target population.

The causal interpretation relies on consistency, Ti=AiTi1+(1−Ai)Ti0T_i=A_iT_i^1+(1-A_i)T_i^0, and on survival transportability: Ti0∣Xi,Ai=1=dTi0∣Xi,Ai=0. T_i^0\mid X_i,A_i=1\ \overset{d}{=}\ T_i^0\mid X_i,A_i=0. Thus, subjects with the same measured covariates must have the same control potential-event-time distribution in the two source populations. The paper also assumes positivity: for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0, 1−π(x)≥ϵ1-\pi(x)\ge\epsilon on the covariate support of the treated population, so that external controls are available for the covariate profiles being targeted. The survival analysis additionally uses independent subjects and the paper’s source-specific independent-censoring conditions. Calibration balances the selected survival features; causal interpretation still depends on these assumptions and the stated marginal proportional hazards model.

1-2. Observed data and notation

Write ℐa={i:Ai=a}\mathcal I_a=\{i:A_i=a\} and na=|ℐa|n_a=|\mathcal I_a| for cohort row indices and sizes. In the simulated example, the source indicator AiA_i is stored in source, the observed follow-up time YiY_i in time, and the event indicator δi\delta_i in event. The baseline covariates XiX_i are age, sex, and marker.

Supplement notation R object Meaning
AiA_i; ℐ0,ℐ1\mathcal I_0,\mathcal I_1 A; I0, I1 Source indicator and cohort row indices
XiX_i; Yi,δiY_i,\delta_i age, sex, marker; time, event Baseline covariates; observed follow-up time and event indicator
KK; κ(i)\kappa(i) K; kappa Number of folds and each subject’s fold
t1,…,tLt_1,\ldots,t_L, L=p−1L=p-1 t_landmark; L, p Landmark times and number of calibration features
ĥi\widehat h_i row i of H Intercept and held-out control-survival predictions
π̂i,q̂i,d̂i\widehat\pi_i,\widehat q_i,\widehat d_i pi_hat, q_hat, d_hat Propensity, odds, and normalized baseline control weights
H0,H1,THH_0,H_1,T_H H0, H1, T_H Cohort-specific feature matrices and target totals
λ,F(λ),J(λ)\lambda,F(\lambda),J(\lambda) lambda, F, J Dual parameter, calibration residual, and Jacobian

Figure 2 shows six rows from the simulated example, linking the cohort labels and survival notation to the columns used by the R code.

library(mecCox)
library(survival)
data(example_external_controls)
dat <- example_external_controls

A <- dat$source
I0 <- which(A == 0L)
I1 <- which(A == 1L)
n <- nrow(dat)
n0 <- length(I0)
n1 <- length(I1)
dat$A <- A
X_names <- c("age", "sex", "marker")

K <- 5L
seed <- 2026L
t_landmark <- c(3, 6, 9, 12, 15)
L <- length(t_landmark)
p <- L + 1L

data.frame(treated = n1, external_controls = n0,
           folds = K, landmarks = L, calibration_features = p)
#>   treated external_controls folds landmarks calibration_features
#> 1     160               320     5         5                    6

Run the code chunks in order. The five landmark times are fixed for this example; the same times and folds will be used in the package comparison.

2. MEC-Cox implementation steps

2-1. [Step 1] Construction of the cross-fitted predictor basis

Partition the pooled sample into KK folds, stratified by AiA_i, and let κ(i)∈{1,…,K}\kappa(i)\in\{1,\ldots,K\} identify the fold containing subject ii. Thus i∈𝒥(κ(i))i\in\mathcal J^{(\kappa(i))}, and the training set for fold kk is 𝒥(−k)={1,…,n}\𝒥(k)\mathcal J^{(-k)}=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal J^{(k)}. For each fold kk, train the control-survival learner using only the external controls in ℐ0∩𝒥(−k)\mathcal I_0\cap\mathcal J^{(-k)}, then evaluate it for all subjects in the held-out fold 𝒥(k)\mathcal J^{(k)}. Define the cross-fitted calibration-feature vector

ĥi=(1,Ŝ0(−κ(i))(t1∣Xi),…,Ŝ0(−κ(i))(tp−1∣Xi))∈ℝp. \widehat h_i= \left(1,\widehat S_0^{(-\kappa(i))}(t_1\mid X_i),\ldots, \widehat S_0^{(-\kappa(i))}(t_{p-1}\mid X_i)\right)\in\mathbb R^p.

Here L=p−1L=p-1 is the number of landmark times. Every non-intercept component is an out-of-sample prediction for subject ii.

Figure 3 shows how each fold is held out in turn to construct these predictions. The same partition also supplies the held-out source-propensity estimates used in Step 2.

The same fold assignment is used for both learners throughout the calculation.

set.seed(seed)
kappa <- integer(n)
for (a in c(0L, 1L)) {
  rows <- which(A == a)
  kappa[rows] <- sample(rep(seq_len(K), length.out = length(rows)))
}

We consider two implementations of the control-survival learner.

  • Cox proportional hazards regression (Cox, 1972; Cox, 1975). Fit the working model among the external-control subjects in the training fold,

    λ0(−k)(t∣X)=λ00(−k)(t)exp⁡{X⊤β0(−k)},i∈ℐ0∩𝒥(−k). \lambda_0^{(-k)}(t\mid X) =\lambda_{00}^{(-k)}(t)\exp\{X^\top\beta_0^{(-k)}\}, \qquad i\in\mathcal I_0\cap\mathcal J^{(-k)}.

    Let β̂0(−k)\widehat\beta_0^{(-k)} and Λ̂00(−k)(t)\widehat\Lambda_{00}^{(-k)}(t) denote its fitted regression coefficient and baseline cumulative hazard estimator. For a validation subject,

    Ŝ0,Cox(−k)(tℓ∣Xi)=exp⁡[−Λ̂00(−k)(tℓ)exp{Xi⊤β̂0(−k)}],ℓ=1,…,L. \widehat S_{0,\mathrm{Cox}}^{(-k)}(t_\ell\mid X_i) =\exp\left[-\widehat\Lambda_{00}^{(-k)}(t_\ell) \exp\{X_i^\top\widehat\beta_0^{(-k)}\}\right], \qquad \ell=1,\ldots,L. 

    predict_survival_cox <- function(training0, validation, fold_seed, settings) {
  survival_formula <- reformulate(X_names, response = "Surv(time, event)")
  outcome_fit <- coxph(
    survival_formula, data = training0,
    ties = "breslow", x = TRUE, singular.ok = FALSE,
    control = coxph.control(timefix = FALSE)
  )
  baseline <- basehaz(outcome_fit, centered = FALSE)
  j <- findInterval(t_landmark, baseline$time)
  Lambda00_hat <- numeric(L)
  Lambda00_hat[j > 0L] <- baseline$hazard[j[j > 0L]]
  lp <- predict(outcome_fit, newdata = validation,
                type = "lp", reference = "zero")
  exp(-outer(exp(lp), Lambda00_hat))
}

    The uncentered linear predictors are paired with the uncentered baseline cumulative hazard. At each landmark, the code uses the most recent cumulative hazard value; before the first event the hazard is zero and survival is one.

  • Random survival forest (RSF) (Ishwaran et al., 2008). Alternatively, fit an RSF on the same external-control training subjects. For each tree b=1,…,Bb=1,\ldots,B, let Λ̂0b(−k)(t∣Xi)\widehat\Lambda_{0b}^{(-k)}(t\mid X_i) denote the terminal-node cumulative hazard estimate for a validation subject. The ranger implementation averages these cumulative hazards and then converts the result to survival:

    Ŝ0,RSF(−k)(tℓ∣Xi)=exp⁡{−1B∑b=1BΛ̂0b(−k)(tℓ∣Xi)},ℓ=1,…,L. \widehat S_{0,\mathrm{RSF}}^{(-k)}(t_\ell\mid X_i) =\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} \widehat\Lambda_{0b}^{(-k)}(t_\ell\mid X_i)\right\}, \qquad \ell=1,\ldots,L.

    This gives a flexible, nonparametric estimate of the conditional control survival function at the same landmark times. The function below uses the forest survival output directly and evaluates its step function at those times.

    predict_survival_rsf <- function(training0, validation, fold_seed, settings) {
  if (!requireNamespace("ranger", quietly = TRUE)) {
    stop("Install ranger to select survival_method = 'rsf'.")
  }
  training_frame <- training0[, c("time", "event", X_names), drop = FALSE]
  forest <- ranger::ranger(
    Surv(time, event) ~ ., data = training_frame,
    num.trees = settings$num_trees,
    min.node.size = settings$min_node_size,
    mtry = max(1L, floor(sqrt(length(X_names)))),
    splitrule = "logrank", num.random.splits = 1L,
    replace = TRUE, sample.fraction = 1,
    write.forest = TRUE, oob.error = FALSE,
    seed = fold_seed, num.threads = 1L
  )
  prediction <- predict(forest,
    data = validation[, X_names, drop = FALSE], num.threads = 1L
  )
  j <- findInterval(t_landmark, prediction$unique.death.times)
  S <- matrix(1, nrow = nrow(validation), ncol = L)
  observed <- which(j > 0L)
  if (length(observed)) {
    S[, observed] <- prediction$survival[, j[observed], drop = FALSE]
  }
  S
}

Choose the survival learner below. The default is Cox; the fixed RSF settings provide an executable alternative for this worked example, with no tuning.

survival_method <- "cox"             # "cox" or "rsf"
rsf_settings <- list(num_trees = 100L, min_node_size = 15L)
predict_survival <- switch(survival_method,
  cox = predict_survival_cox, rsf = predict_survival_rsf,
  stop("Choose survival_method from cox and rsf.")
)
S0_hat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n, ncol = L)
for (k in seq_len(K)) {
  train0 <- which(kappa != k & A == 0L)
  valid <- which(kappa == k)
  S0_hat[valid, ] <- predict_survival(
    dat[train0, ], dat[valid, ], as.integer(seed + k), rsf_settings
  )
}
colnames(S0_hat) <- paste0("S0(t=", t_landmark, ")")
H <- cbind(intercept = 1, S0_hat)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(H)), all(S0_hat >= 0 & S0_hat <= 1))

In both cases, the predictor basis summarizes the estimated counterfactual control-survival profile for each subject and is used only as a calibration feature. The final Cox model in Step 6 uses AiA_i as its sole regression covariate.

2-2. [Step 2] Baseline ATT odds weights

We next construct the baseline weights around which the MEC calibration is performed. Using the same folds as in Step 1, estimate the source propensity score

π(Xi)=Pr⁡(Ai=1∣Xi) \pi(X_i)=\Pr(A_i=1\mid X_i)

on the pooled training sample 𝒥(−k)\mathcal J^{(-k)}. Write the fitted learner as π̂(−k)(X)\widehat\pi^{(-k)}(X). For a subject in the held-out fold i∈𝒥(k)i\in\mathcal J^{(k)}, the cross-fitted prediction is

π̂i=π̂(−k)(Xi), \widehat\pi_i=\widehat\pi^{(-k)}(X_i),

possibly truncated away from zero and one. Thus, each subject’s prediction is obtained without using that subject to train the propensity learner.

For external-control subjects i∈ℐ0i\in\mathcal I_0, form the estimated ATT odds and normalize them to have total mass equal to the treated cohort size:

q̂i=π̂i1−π̂i,d̂i=n1q̂i∑j∈ℐ0q̂j,∑i∈ℐ0d̂i=n1. \widehat q_i=\frac{\widehat\pi_i}{1-\widehat\pi_i}, \qquad \widehat d_i=\frac{n_1\widehat q_i} {\sum_{j\in\mathcal I_0}\widehat q_j}, \qquad \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0}\widehat d_i=n_1.

These normalized odds weights are the baseline for the Bregman calibration in Step 3. We consider two implementations of the source propensity-score learner.

  • Logistic regression. The GLM working model is

    πγ(Xi)=exp⁡(γ⊤X̃i)1+exp⁡(γ⊤X̃i), \pi_\gamma(X_i) =\frac{\exp(\gamma^\top\widetilde X_i)} {1+\exp(\gamma^\top\widetilde X_i)},

    where X̃i\widetilde X_i contains an intercept and the selected baseline covariates. Fitting it on 𝒥(−k)\mathcal J^{(-k)} gives γ̂(−k)\widehat\gamma^{(-k)}, and the held-out prediction is

    π̂glm(−k)(Xi)=exp⁡{(γ̂(−k))⊤X̃i}1+exp⁡{(γ̂(−k))⊤X̃i}. \widehat\pi^{(-k)}_{\mathrm{glm}}(X_i) =\frac{\exp\{(\widehat\gamma^{(-k)})^\top\widetilde X_i\}} {1+\exp\{(\widehat\gamma^{(-k)})^\top\widetilde X_i\}}. 

    predict_ps_glm <- function(training, validation, fold_seed, settings) {
  fit <- glm(reformulate(X_names, response = "A"),
             data = training, family = binomial())
  stopifnot(isTRUE(fit$converged), all(is.finite(coef(fit))))
  as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = validation, type = "response"))
}

  • Flexible machine-learning classifier. Alternatively, train a binary classifier on the same pooled training sample. Examples include deep learning (DL) (LeCun et al., 2015), random forest (Breiman, 2001), and Bayesian additive regression trees (BART; Chipman et al., 2010). Each produces the held-out estimate

    π̂ML(−k)(Xi)=Pr̂(Ai=1∣Xi). \widehat\pi^{(-k)}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X_i) =\widehat{\Pr}(A_i=1\mid X_i).

    The functions below implement these alternatives directly. "glm" remains the default; changing ps_method selects one learner. The fixed settings are for this worked example, with no tuning. The optional packages are needed only when their corresponding learner is selected. The DL option also needs the torch runtime installed.

    ps_method <- "glm"                 # "glm", "rf", "bart", or "mlp"
ps_trim <- c(0.01, 0.99)
ps_settings <- list(
  rf_trees = 100L, rf_min_node_size = 5L,
  bart_trees = 50L, bart_draws = 500L, bart_burn_in = 200L,
  bart_shrinkage = 2,
  mlp_hidden_units = c(16L, 8L), mlp_epochs = 50L
)

    BART and DL use numeric predictor matrices. Factor coding is determined from the training fold and applied unchanged to the validation fold. Validation subjects do not determine factor levels or scaling values.

    ps_predictor_matrices <- function(training, validation) {
  training <- training[, X_names, drop = FALSE]
  validation <- validation[, X_names, drop = FALSE]
  for (name in X_names) {
    if (is.factor(training[[name]]) || is.character(training[[name]])) {
      train_factor <- droplevels(factor(training[[name]]))
      observed_levels <- levels(train_factor)
      if (length(observed_levels) < 2L ||
          any(!as.character(validation[[name]]) %in% observed_levels)) {
        stop("A validation factor level is absent from its training fold.")
      }
      training[[name]] <- train_factor
      validation[[name]] <- factor(as.character(validation[[name]]),
                                   levels = observed_levels)
    }
  }
  formula <- reformulate(X_names)
  x_train <- model.matrix(formula, training)[, -1L, drop = FALSE]
  x_valid <- model.matrix(formula, validation)[, -1L, drop = FALSE]
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(x_train), colnames(x_valid)))
  list(training = x_train, validation = x_valid)
}

    • Random forest (ps_method = "rf").

      The random-forest classifier returns the probability of source group 1.

      predict_ps_rf <- function(training, validation, fold_seed, settings) {
  if (!requireNamespace("ranger", quietly = TRUE)) {
    stop("Install ranger to select ps_method = 'rf'.")
  }
  training$A_factor <- factor(training$A, levels = c(0, 1))
  fit <- ranger::ranger(
    reformulate(X_names, response = "A_factor"), data = training,
    probability = TRUE, num.trees = settings$rf_trees,
    min.node.size = settings$rf_min_node_size,
    mtry = max(1L, floor(sqrt(length(X_names)))),
    seed = fold_seed, num.threads = 1L, oob.error = FALSE
  )
  as.numeric(predict(fit, data = validation[, X_names, drop = FALSE],
                     num.threads = 1L)$predictions[, "1"])
}

    • Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) (ps_method = "bart").

      For binary BART with a probit link, probabilities are averaged over posterior draws. The offset is supplied once when fitting; the returned latent draws already include it.

      predict_ps_bart <- function(training, validation, fold_seed, settings) {
  if (!requireNamespace("dbarts", quietly = TRUE)) {
    stop("Install dbarts to select ps_method = 'bart'.")
  }
  x <- ps_predictor_matrices(training, validation)
  source_fraction <- min(max(mean(training$A), 0.01), 0.99)
  fit <- dbarts::bart(
    x.train = x$training, y.train = training$A, x.test = x$validation,
    ntree = settings$bart_trees, ndpost = settings$bart_draws,
    nskip = settings$bart_burn_in, k = settings$bart_shrinkage,
    binaryOffset = qnorm(source_fraction),
    seed = fold_seed, nthread = 1L, verbose = FALSE,
    keeptrees = FALSE, keeptrainfits = FALSE
  )
  if (!is.null(fit$prob.test.mean)) {
    return(as.numeric(fit$prob.test.mean))
  }
  if (!is.null(fit$prob.test)) {
    return(as.numeric(colMeans(fit$prob.test)))
  }
  latent_draws <- fit[["yhat.test"]]
  if (is.null(latent_draws)) {
    stop("The BART fit did not return posterior validation predictions.")
  }
  as.numeric(colMeans(pnorm(latent_draws)))
}

    • Deep learning (DL) (ps_method = "mlp").

      The worked example uses a feedforward multilayer perceptron (MLP). For the DL model, predictor means and standard deviations are computed on the training fold. The same transformation is applied to held-out subjects. The two hidden layers use ReLU activations; the output is the estimated probability of source group 1. Its internal validation subset is drawn only from the outer training fold.

      predict_ps_mlp <- function(training, validation, fold_seed, settings) {
  if (!requireNamespace("brulee", quietly = TRUE) ||
      !requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE)) {
    stop("Install brulee and torch to select ps_method = 'mlp'.")
  }
  x <- ps_predictor_matrices(training, validation)
  center <- colMeans(x$training)
  spread <- apply(x$training, 2L, sd)
  spread[!is.finite(spread) | spread < 1e-12] <- 1
  train_frame <- as.data.frame(scale(x$training, center, spread))
  valid_frame <- as.data.frame(scale(x$validation, center, spread))
  names(train_frame) <- names(valid_frame) <-
    make.names(names(train_frame), unique = TRUE)
  train_frame$A <- factor(training$A, levels = c(0, 1))

  old_threads <- torch::torch_get_num_threads()
  old_state <- torch::torch_get_rng_state()
  on.exit({
    torch::torch_set_rng_state(old_state)
    torch::torch_set_num_threads(old_threads)
  }, add = TRUE)
  torch::torch_set_num_threads(1L)
  torch::torch_manual_seed(fold_seed)
  fit <- brulee::brulee_mlp(
    A ~ ., data = train_frame,
    hidden_units = settings$mlp_hidden_units,
    epochs = settings$mlp_epochs, activation = "relu",
    optimizer = "ADAMw", learn_rate = 0.01,
    penalty = 0.001, dropout = 0.1,
    batch_size = min(128L, nrow(train_frame)),
    validation = 0.1, stop_iter = 10L,
    device = "cpu", verbose = FALSE
  )
  as.numeric(predict(fit, new_data = valid_frame, type = "prob")[[".pred_1"]])
}

The common fold loop below applies the selected learner to 𝒥(−k)\mathcal J^{(-k)} and evaluates it on 𝒥(k)\mathcal J^{(k)}. The fold-specific seed controls stochastic learners; it does not change the shared fold assignment kappa constructed in Step 1.

with_ps_seed <- function(value, expression) {
  had_seed <- exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)
  if (had_seed) old_seed <- get(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv)
  on.exit({
    if (had_seed) assign(".Random.seed", old_seed, envir = .GlobalEnv)
    else if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)) {
      rm(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv)
    }
  }, add = TRUE)
  set.seed(value)
  force(expression)
}
predict_ps <- switch(ps_method,
  glm = predict_ps_glm, rf = predict_ps_rf,
  bart = predict_ps_bart, mlp = predict_ps_mlp,
  stop("Choose ps_method from glm, rf, bart, and mlp.")
)
pi_hat <- numeric(n)
for (k in seq_len(K)) {
  train <- which(kappa != k)
  valid <- which(kappa == k)
  fold_seed <- as.integer(seed + k)
  held_out <- with_ps_seed(fold_seed,
    predict_ps(dat[train, ], dat[valid, ], fold_seed, ps_settings)
  )
  stopifnot(length(held_out) == length(valid), all(is.finite(held_out)),
            all(held_out >= 0 & held_out <= 1))
  pi_hat[valid] <- held_out
}
pi_hat <- pmin(pmax(pi_hat, ps_trim[1]), ps_trim[2])

Using the held-out predictions, compute the normalized baseline weights defined above.

q_hat <- pi_hat[I0] / (1 - pi_hat[I0])
d_hat <- n1 * q_hat / sum(q_hat)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(d_hat)), all(d_hat > 0))
c(baseline_weight_total = sum(d_hat), treated_count = n1)
#> baseline_weight_total         treated_count
#>                   160                   160

d_hat contains external-control weights only, in the order of I0; changing the propensity learner leaves this construction unchanged.

2-3. [Step 3] Formulation of the primal problem

Write the index sets as

ℐ0={i10,…,in00},ℐ1={i11,…,in11}, \mathcal I_0=\{i_1^0,\ldots,i_{n_0}^0\}, \qquad \mathcal I_1=\{i_1^1,\ldots,i_{n_1}^1\},

where im0i_m^0 denotes the index of the mmth external-control subject and im1i_m^1 denotes the index of the mmth treated subject.

Stacking the vectors ĥi\widehat h_i obtained in Step 1 as rows within each cohort, define the calibration-feature matrices

H0=(ĥi10⋮ĥin00)=(1Ŝ0(−κ(i10))(t1∣Xi10)⋯Ŝ0(−κ(i10))(tp−1∣Xi10)⋮⋮⋱⋮1Ŝ0(−κ(in00))(t1∣Xin00)⋯Ŝ0(−κ(in00))(tp−1∣Xin00))∈ℝn0×p, H_0 = \begin{pmatrix} \widehat h_{i_1^0}\\ \vdots\\ \widehat h_{i_{n_0}^0} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \widehat S_0^{(-\kappa(i_1^0))}(t_1\mid X_{i_1^0}) & \cdots & \widehat S_0^{(-\kappa(i_1^0))}(t_{p-1}\mid X_{i_1^0})\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ 1 & \widehat S_0^{(-\kappa(i_{n_0}^0))}(t_1\mid X_{i_{n_0}^0}) & \cdots & \widehat S_0^{(-\kappa(i_{n_0}^0))}(t_{p-1}\mid X_{i_{n_0}^0}) \end{pmatrix} \in\mathbb R^{n_0\times p},

and

H1=(ĥi11⋮ĥin11)=(1Ŝ0(−κ(i11))(t1∣Xi11)⋯Ŝ0(−κ(i11))(tp−1∣Xi11)⋮⋮⋱⋮1Ŝ0(−κ(in11))(t1∣Xin11)⋯Ŝ0(−κ(in11))(tp−1∣Xin11))∈ℝn1×p. H_1 = \begin{pmatrix} \widehat h_{i_1^1}\\ \vdots\\ \widehat h_{i_{n_1}^1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \widehat S_0^{(-\kappa(i_1^1))}(t_1\mid X_{i_1^1}) & \cdots & \widehat S_0^{(-\kappa(i_1^1))}(t_{p-1}\mid X_{i_1^1})\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ 1 & \widehat S_0^{(-\kappa(i_{n_1}^1))}(t_1\mid X_{i_{n_1}^1}) & \cdots & \widehat S_0^{(-\kappa(i_{n_1}^1))}(t_{p-1}\mid X_{i_{n_1}^1}) \end{pmatrix} \in\mathbb R^{n_1\times p}.

Here H0H_0 contains the cross-fitted control-survival features for external-control subjects, whereas H1H_1 contains the same features evaluated at the covariate values of treated subjects.

The target calibration total is then expressed as the pp-dimensional vector

TH=H1⊤𝟏n1=∑i∈ℐ1ĥi∈ℝp. T_H = H_1^\top \mathbf 1_{n_1} = \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_1}\widehat h_i \in \mathbb{R}^{p}.

For i∈ℐ0i\in\mathcal I_0, let d̂i\widehat d_i denote the normalized baseline ATT odds weight,

d̂i=n1q̂i∑j∈ℐ0q̂j,q̂i=π̂i1−π̂i=π̂(−k)(Xi)1−π̂(−k)(Xi), \widehat d_i = \frac{n_1\widehat q_i} {\sum_{j\in\mathcal I_0}\widehat q_j}, \qquad \widehat q_i = \frac{\widehat\pi_i}{1-\widehat\pi_i} = \frac{\widehat\pi^{(-k)}(X_i)}{1-\widehat\pi^{(-k)}(X_i)},

where k=κ(i)k=\kappa(i) and π̂i\widehat\pi_i is obtained in Step 2.

The MEC-Cox calibrated weights are obtained by the Bregman projection

ŵ=arg⁡min{wi>0:i∈ℐ0}∑i∈ℐ0DG(wi∥d̂i) \widehat w = \arg\min_{\{w_i>0:i\in\mathcal I_0\}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0} D_G(w_i\|\widehat d_i)

subject to

H0⊤w=H1⊤𝟏n1=TH∈ℝp, H_0^\top w = H_1^\top\mathbf 1_{n_1} = T_H\in \mathbb{R}^{p},

where

DG(wi∥d̂i)=G(wi)−G(d̂i)−g(d̂i)(wi−d̂i),g=G′, D_G(w_i\|\widehat d_i) = G(w_i)-G(\widehat d_i)-g(\widehat d_i)(w_i-\widehat d_i), \qquad g=G',

and GG is a strictly convex generator.

Directly solving this primal problem would require optimizing over n0n_0 external-control weights. Instead, MEC-Cox solves the equivalent low-dimensional dual problem, whose dimension is only pp, the number of calibration features.

The intercept constraint preserves the total external-control weight n1n_1; the other constraints match the treated cohort’s predicted-survival totals. The following code constructs these matrices and uses the KL generator G(u)=ulog⁡uG(u)=u\log u for the worked example.

H0 <- H[I0, , drop = FALSE]
H1 <- H[I1, , drop = FALSE]
T_H <- colSums(H1)

# KL generator from the manuscript: G(u) = u log(u), for u > 0.
G <- function(u) u * log(u)
g <- function(u) 1 + log(u)
g_inv <- function(v) exp(v - 1)
g_prime <- function(u) 1 / u

data.frame(feature = colnames(H),
           treated_total = T_H,
           baseline_control_total = as.numeric(crossprod(H0, d_hat)),
           row.names = NULL)
#>     feature treated_total baseline_control_total
#> 1 intercept      160.0000               160.0000
#> 2   S0(t=3)      140.4550               140.9055
#> 3   S0(t=6)      122.9990               123.6722
#> 4   S0(t=9)      104.3938               105.3782
#> 5  S0(t=12)       94.0362                95.0081
#> 6  S0(t=15)       83.2960                84.4723

2-4. [Step 4] Conversion to the dual problem

We next convert the constrained primal problem into a low-dimensional dual problem. Recall that the MEC-Cox calibration problem is

ŵ=arg⁡min{wi>0:i∈ℐ0}∑i∈ℐ0DG(wi∥d̂i)subject toH0⊤w=TH∈ℝp. \widehat w = \arg\min_{\{w_i>0:i\in\mathcal I_0\}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0} D_G(w_i\|\widehat d_i) \quad \text{subject to} \quad H_0^\top w=T_H \in \mathbb{R}^{p}.

Let λ∈ℝp\lambda\in\mathbb R^p denote the Lagrange multiplier associated with the calibration constraint. Define the Lagrangian

ℒ(w,λ)=∑i∈ℐ0DG(wi∥d̂i)−λ⊤(H0⊤w−TH). \mathcal L(w,\lambda) = \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0} D_G(w_i\|\widehat d_i) - \lambda^\top \left( H_0^\top w - T_H \right).

Because

DG(wi∥d̂i)=G(wi)−G(d̂i)−g(d̂i)(wi−d̂i),g=G′, D_G(w_i\|\widehat d_i) = G(w_i)-G(\widehat d_i)-g(\widehat d_i)(w_i-\widehat d_i), \qquad g=G',

we have

∂∂wiDG(wi∥d̂i)=g(wi)−g(d̂i). \frac{\partial}{\partial w_i} D_G(w_i\|\widehat d_i) = g(w_i)-g(\widehat d_i).

Therefore, the stationarity condition of the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) equations is

∂ℒ(w,λ)∂wi=g(wi)−g(d̂i)−λ⊤ĥi=0,i∈ℐ0. \frac{\partial \mathcal L(w,\lambda)}{\partial w_i} = g(w_i)-g(\widehat d_i)-\lambda^\top\widehat h_i = 0, \qquad i\in\mathcal I_0.

Equivalently,

g(wi)=g(d̂i)+λ⊤ĥi. g(w_i) = g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda^\top\widehat h_i.

Since GG is strictly convex, g=G′g=G' is strictly increasing and hence invertible on its domain. Thus, for any fixed admissible λ\lambda, the primal weight satisfying the stationarity condition is

wi(λ)=g−1{g(d̂i)+λ⊤ĥi},i∈ℐ0. w_i(\lambda) = g^{-1}\{g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda^\top\widehat h_i\}, \qquad i\in\mathcal I_0.

The remaining KKT condition is primal feasibility

H0⊤w(λ)=TH. H_0^\top w(\lambda)=T_H.

Substituting the dual representation wi(λ)w_i(\lambda) into the calibration constraint yields the dual estimating equation

F(λ)=∑i∈ℐ0wi(λ)ĥi−TH=0. F(\lambda) = \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0} w_i(\lambda)\widehat h_i - T_H = 0.

Equivalently,

F(λ)=∑i∈ℐ0ĥig−1{g(d̂i)+λ⊤ĥi}−∑i∈ℐ1ĥi=0, F(\lambda) = \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0} \widehat h_i g^{-1}\{g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda^\top\widehat h_i\} - \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_1}\widehat h_i = 0,

or, in matrix form,

F(λ)=H0⊤w(λ)−TH. F(\lambda) = H_0^\top w(\lambda)-T_H.

Thus, instead of optimizing over the n0n_0-dimensional vector ww, MEC-Cox solves the pp-dimensional nonlinear equation F(λ)=0F(\lambda)=0.

The dual estimating equation also supplies the calibration component of the stacked system for variance estimation.

For the KL choice used in the code, g(u)=1+log⁡ug(u)=1+\log u and g−1(v)=exp⁡(v−1)g^{-1}(v)=\exp(v-1). Consequently,

wi(λ)=d̂iexp⁡(λ⊤ĥi). w_i(\lambda)=\widehat d_i\exp(\lambda^\top\widehat h_i).

The functions below evaluate the implied weights and the dual residual. At λ=0\lambda=0, the implied weights are the baseline weights.

w_of_lambda <- function(lambda) {
  nu <- g(d_hat) + as.numeric(H0 %*% lambda)
  g_inv(nu)
}

F <- function(lambda) {
  as.numeric(crossprod(H0, w_of_lambda(lambda)) - T_H)
}

lambda0 <- numeric(p)
stopifnot(max(abs(w_of_lambda(lambda0) - d_hat)) < 1e-12)

2-5. [Step 5] Dual Newton solver

The Newton update is based on the Jacobian of F(λ)F(\lambda). We view the dual calibration map as

F:𝒟λ⊆ℝp→ℝp, F:\mathcal D_{\lambda}\subseteq \mathbb R^{p}\longrightarrow \mathbb R^{p},

where

𝒟λ={λ∈ℝp:g(d̂i)+λ⊤ĥi∈dom(g−1)for all i∈ℐ0}. \mathcal D_{\lambda} = \left\{ \lambda\in\mathbb R^{p}: g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda^\top \widehat h_i \in \operatorname{dom}(g^{-1}) \ \text{for all } i\in\mathcal I_0 \right\}.

That is, the domain of FF consists of all dual parameters λ\lambda for which the implied weights wi(λ)=g−1{g(d̂i)+λ⊤ĥi},w_i(\lambda) = g^{-1}\{g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda^\top \widehat h_i\}, (i∈ℐ0)(i\in\mathcal I_0) are well-defined.

By the stationarity equation in Step 4, let

νi(λ)=g(d̂i)+λ⊤ĥi,wi(λ)=g−1{νi(λ)}. \nu_i(\lambda) = g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda^\top\widehat h_i, \qquad w_i(\lambda)=g^{-1}\{\nu_i(\lambda)\}.

Assuming g′(w)>0g'(w)>0 at the weights considered, the inverse-function derivative is

∂wi(λ)∂νi=1g′{wi(λ)}, \frac{\partial w_i(\lambda)}{\partial \nu_i} = \frac{1}{g'\{w_i(\lambda)\}},

and hence the Jacobian of F(λ)F(\lambda) is

J(λ)=∂F(λ)∂λ⊤=∑i∈ℐ01g′{wi(λ)}ĥiĥi⊤∈ℝp×p. J(\lambda) = \frac{\partial F(\lambda)}{\partial \lambda^\top} = \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0} \frac{1}{g'\{w_i(\lambda)\}} \widehat h_i\widehat h_i^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}.

In matrix form,

J(λ)=H0⊤diag⁡[1g′{wi(λ)}:i∈ℐ0]H0∈ℝp×p. J(\lambda) = H_0^\top \operatorname{diag} \left[ \frac{1}{g'\{w_i(\lambda)\}}:i\in\mathcal I_0 \right] H_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}.

At iteration mm, the Newton direction Δm\Delta_m solves

{J(λm)+ρIp}Δm=F(λm), \{J(\lambda_m)+\rho I_{p}\}\Delta_m = F(\lambda_m),

where ρ>0\rho>0 is a small ridge constant used for numerical stability. The dual parameter is updated by

λm+1=λm−αmΔm=λm−αm{J(λm)+ρIp}−1F(λm), \lambda_{m+1} = \lambda_m-\alpha_m\Delta_m= \lambda_m-\alpha_m \{J(\lambda_m)+\rho I_{p}\}^{-1}F(\lambda_m),

where αm∈(0,1]\alpha_m\in(0,1] is chosen by step-halving if necessary to keep all dual arguments νi(λm+1)=g(d̂i)+λm+1⊤ĥi\nu_i(\lambda_{m+1}) = g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda_{m+1}^\top\widehat h_i inside the domain of g−1g^{-1}. The iteration stops when the calibration residual is sufficiently small, for example when

∥F(λm)∥2=∥H0⊤w(λm)−TH∥2≤ε \|F(\lambda_m)\|_2 = \left\| H_0^\top w(\lambda_m)-T_H \right\|_2 \le \varepsilon

for a prespecified tolerance ε\varepsilon.

The ridge constant ρ\rho, the step-halving rule, and the stopping tolerance ε\varepsilon are user-specified numerical choices. For the illustrative solver below, we use ρ=10−8\rho=10^{-8}, initialize αm=1\alpha_m=1, and apply step-halving only when necessary to keep the dual argument within the domain of g−1g^{-1}. The stopping tolerance is ε=10−10\varepsilon=10^{-10}, with at most 100 Newton iterations.

For the KL generator, 1/g′(wi)=wi1/g'(w_i)=w_i and dom⁡(g−1)=ℝ\operatorname{dom}(g^{-1})=\mathbb R. The step-halving guard in the code also rejects weights that overflow or underflow in finite-precision arithmetic. It starts each update with αm=1\alpha_m=1, then halves the step until the implied weights are finite and positive.

J <- function(lambda) {
  w <- w_of_lambda(lambda)
  crossprod(H0, H0 * (1 / g_prime(w)))
}

rho <- 1e-8
epsilon <- 1e-10
max_iter <- 100L
lambda <- lambda0
converged <- FALSE
history <- data.frame(iteration = integer(), residual_L2 = numeric())

for (m in 0:max_iter) {
  residual <- F(lambda)
  residual_L2 <- sqrt(sum(residual^2))
  history <- rbind(history, data.frame(iteration = m,
                                      residual_L2 = residual_L2))
  if (is.finite(residual_L2) && residual_L2 <= epsilon) {
    converged <- TRUE
    break
  }
  if (m == max_iter) break

  Delta <- solve(J(lambda) + rho * diag(p), residual)
  alpha <- 1
  accepted <- FALSE
  for (halving in 0:60) {
    candidate <- lambda - alpha * Delta
    w_candidate <- w_of_lambda(candidate)
    if (all(is.finite(w_candidate)) && all(w_candidate > 0)) {
      accepted <- TRUE
      break
    }
    alpha <- alpha / 2
  }
  if (!accepted) stop("No admissible Newton step was found.")
  lambda <- candidate
}

if (!converged) stop("The dual solver did not reach the stated tolerance.")
lambda_hat <- lambda
w_hat <- w_of_lambda(lambda_hat)
history
#>   iteration residual_L2
#> 1         0 1.98840e+00
#> 2         1 3.02732e+00
#> 3         2 5.82436e-02
#> 4         3 3.65760e-05
#> 5         4 1.96874e-11

The balance table makes the constraint H0⊤ŵ=THH_0^\top\widehat w=T_H visible.

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  feature = colnames(H),
  treated_mean = T_H / n1,
  baseline_control_mean = as.numeric(crossprod(H0, d_hat)) / n1,
  calibrated_control_mean = as.numeric(crossprod(H0, w_hat)) / n1
), digits = 6, row.names = FALSE,
col.names = c("Feature", "Treated mean", "Baseline control mean",
              "Calibrated control mean"))
Feature Treated mean Baseline control mean Calibrated control mean
intercept 1.000000 1.000000 1.000000
S0(t=3) 0.877844 0.880659 0.877844
S0(t=6) 0.768744 0.772951 0.768744
S0(t=9) 0.652461 0.658614 0.652461
S0(t=12) 0.587726 0.593801 0.587726
S0(t=15) 0.520600 0.527952 0.520600

The dual formulation solves for pp calibration parameters instead of n0n_0 external-control weights. Its parameter dimension is pp, although forming the Jacobian still requires contributions from all n0n_0 external-control subjects. At each iteration, assembling the p×pp\times p Jacobian J(λ)J(\lambda) requires O(n0p2)O(n_0p^2) operations, and solving for the Newton step requires O(p3)O(p^3) operations.

2-6. [Step 6] Final MEC-Cox estimator

After convergence of the dual Newton solver, let λ̂\widehat\lambda denote the resulting dual solution and define the calibrated external-control weights by

ŵi=g−1{g(d̂i)+λ̂⊤ĥi},i∈ℐ0. \widehat w_i = g^{-1}\{g(\widehat d_i)+\widehat\lambda^\top \widehat h_i\}, \qquad i\in \mathcal I_0 .

The final MEC-Cox estimating-equation weight is

ω̃i={1,i∈ℐ1(treated cohort),ŵi,i∈ℐ0(external-control cohort). \widetilde\omega_i = \begin{cases} 1, & i\in\mathcal I_1 \quad \text{(treated cohort)},\\ \widehat w_i, & i\in\mathcal I_0 \quad \text{(external-control cohort)}. \end{cases}

Here, we write ω̃i\widetilde\omega_i for ω̃i(λ̂)\widetilde\omega_i(\widehat\lambda), suppressing dependence on the fitted dual parameter for notational simplicity. The tilde distinguishes it from the logistic IPW weight ω̂i(γ̂)\widehat\omega_i(\widehat\gamma).

Here 𝒴i(t)\mathcal Y_i(t) is the at-risk indicator and 𝒩i(t)\mathcal N_i(t) is the event counting process. Using the final weights, define

SMEC,ω̃(r)(t;θ)=∑i=1nω̃i𝒴i(t)exp⁡(θAi)Air,r=0,1, S_{\mathrm{MEC},\widetilde\omega}^{(r)}(t;\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \widetilde\omega_i \mathcal{Y}_i(t)\exp(\theta A_i)A_i^r, \qquad r=0,1,

and

A¯MEC,ω̃(t;θ)=SMEC,ω̃(1)(t;θ)SMEC,ω̃(0)(t;θ). \overline A_{\mathrm{MEC},\widetilde\omega}(t;\theta) = \frac{S_{\mathrm{MEC},\widetilde\omega}^{(1)}(t;\theta)} {S_{\mathrm{MEC},\widetilde\omega}^{(0)}(t;\theta)} .

The MEC-Cox estimator is the solution to the weighted Cox estimating equation

UnMEC(θ)=Unω̃(θ)=∑i=1n∫ω̃i{Ai−A¯MEC,ω̃(t;θ)}d𝒩i(t)=0. U_n^{\mathrm{MEC}}(\theta) =U_n^{\widetilde\omega}(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \int \widetilde\omega_i \{A_i-\overline A_{\mathrm{MEC},\widetilde\omega}(t;\theta)\} \,d\mathcal{N}_i(t) = 0.

Equivalently, θ̂MEC\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MEC}} maximizes the weighted Cox partial log-likelihood

ℓMEC(θ)=∑i=1nω̃i∫[θAi−log{SMEC,ω̃(0)(t;θ)}]d𝒩i(t). \ell_{\mathrm{MEC}}(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \widetilde\omega_i \int \left[ \theta A_i - \log\{S_{\mathrm{MEC},\widetilde\omega}^{(0)}(t;\theta)\} \right] \,d\mathcal{N}_i(t).

The final MEC-Cox hazard-ratio estimator is therefore

HR̂MEC=exp⁡(θ̂MEC). \widehat{\mathrm{HR}}_{\mathrm{MEC}} = \exp(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MEC}}).

In R, the point estimate is obtained by fitting a weighted Cox model with A as its sole covariate. Breslow handling of tied events matches the package.

omega_tilde <- rep(1, n)
omega_tilde[I0] <- w_hat
dat$omega_tilde <- omega_tilde

final_fit <- coxph(
  Surv(time, event) ~ A, data = dat, weights = omega_tilde,
  ties = "breslow", robust = FALSE,
  control = coxph.control(timefix = FALSE)
)
theta_hat <- unname(coef(final_fit)["A"])
HR_hat <- exp(theta_hat)
data.frame(log_hazard_ratio = theta_hat, hazard_ratio = HR_hat)
#>   log_hazard_ratio hazard_ratio
#> 1        0.0899067      1.09407

This step illustrates the point estimator. For the MEC stacked-sandwich standard error and confidence interval, use fit_mec_cox() as below; the ordinary weighted coxph() standard error is not that variance estimator.

3. Algorithm summary

Algorithm S1. Computational algorithm for the MEC-Cox estimator

  1. Partition the pooled sample into KK folds, stratified by the source indicator AiA_i.

  2. For each validation subject i∈𝒥(k)i\in\mathcal J^{(k)}, compute cross-fitted nuisance estimates

    π̂i=π̂(−k)(Xi),ĥi=(1,Ŝ0(−k)(t1∣Xi),…,Ŝ0(−k)(tp−1∣Xi)), \widehat\pi_i=\widehat\pi^{(-k)}(X_i), \qquad \widehat h_i= \left(1,\widehat S_0^{(-k)}(t_1\mid X_i),\ldots, \widehat S_0^{(-k)}(t_{p-1}\mid X_i)\right),

    where π̂(−k)\widehat\pi^{(-k)} is trained on 𝒥(−k)\mathcal J^{(-k)}, and Ŝ0(−k)\widehat S_0^{(-k)} is trained using external controls in ℐ0∩𝒥(−k)\mathcal I_0\cap\mathcal J^{(-k)}.

  3. For i∈ℐ0i\in\mathcal I_0, define the normalized baseline ATT odds weight

    d̂i=n1q̂i∑j∈ℐ0q̂j,q̂i=π̂i1−π̂i. \widehat d_i= \frac{n_1\widehat q_i}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal I_0}\widehat q_j}, \qquad \widehat q_i=\frac{\widehat\pi_i}{1-\widehat\pi_i}.

  4. Solve the dual calibration equation

    F(λ)=∑i∈ℐ0ĥig−1{g(d̂i)+λ⊤ĥi}−∑i∈ℐ1ĥi=0 F(\lambda)= \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0} \widehat h_i g^{-1}\{g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda^\top\widehat h_i\} -\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_1}\widehat h_i=0

    by a damped Newton solver, and denote the solution by λ̂\widehat\lambda.

  5. Recover the MEC-updated external-control weights and the final estimating-equation weights:

    ŵi=g−1{g(d̂i)+λ̂⊤ĥi},i∈ℐ0, \widehat w_i= g^{-1}\{g(\widehat d_i)+\widehat\lambda^\top\widehat h_i\}, \qquad i\in\mathcal I_0,

    ω̃i=ω̃i(λ̂)={1,i∈ℐ1,ŵi,i∈ℐ0. \widetilde\omega_i= \widetilde\omega_i(\widehat\lambda)= \begin{cases} 1, & i\in\mathcal I_1,\\ \widehat w_i, & i\in\mathcal I_0. \end{cases}

  6. Report HR̂MEC=exp⁡(θ̂MEC)\widehat{\mathrm{HR}}_{\mathrm{MEC}}=\exp(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MEC}}) by solving

    UnMEC(θ)=Unω̃(θ)=∑i=1n∫ω̃i{Ai−A¯MEC,ω̃(t;θ)}d𝒩i(t)=0. U_n^{\mathrm{MEC}}(\theta)= U_n^{\widetilde\omega}(\theta)= \sum_{i=1}^n\int\widetilde\omega_i \{A_i-\overline A_{\mathrm{MEC},\widetilde\omega}(t;\theta)\} \,d\mathcal N_i(t)=0.

Algorithm lines 1–3 construct the inputs developed in Steps 1–2 above; line 4 combines Steps 3–5; and lines 5–6 give the final calculation in Step 6.

4. More technical details

4-1. Agreement with fit_mec_cox()

The package call performs calibration and estimation using the same inputs. We pass the cross-fitted propensity scores from Step 2 through ps_predictions, so the selected classifier is not fitted again. The package reconstructs the same folds from seed and fits the selected Cox or RSF survival learner with the same landmark times and settings.

Choose kl_derivative = "numerical" (default) or "analytic" for the KL cross-derivative used in the sandwich variance. The detailed KL cross-derivative illustration below derives both choices and compares them using this fitted example.

# Choose one KL cross-derivative calculation; numerical is the default.
kl_derivative <- "numerical"  # Change to "analytic" for the analytic calculation.

mec <- fit_mec_cox(
  example_external_controls,
  time = "time", event = "event", source = "source",
  covariates = X_names, ps_predictions = pi_hat,
  survival_learner = survival_method,
  kl_derivative = kl_derivative,
  n_folds = K, landmarks = t_landmark, seed = seed, ps_trim = ps_trim,
  nuisance_settings = "standard", rsf_auto_tune = FALSE,
  rsf_num_trees = rsf_settings$num_trees,
  rsf_min_node_size = rsf_settings$min_node_size
)

# First verify the ingredients, before comparing the calibrated estimates.
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(mec$ps_predictions_supplied),
  identical(kappa, mec$fold_id),
  max(abs(pi_hat - mec$ps_oof)) < 1e-12,
  max(abs(H - mec$basis)) < 1e-12,
  max(abs(d_hat - mec$baseline_weights[I0])) < 1e-12
)

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  calculation = c("Steps 1-6", "fit_mec_cox()"),
  log_hazard_ratio = c(theta_hat, mec$theta),
  hazard_ratio = c(HR_hat, mec$hr),
  control_weight_total = c(sum(w_hat), sum(mec$weights[I0])),
  max_mean_balance_residual = format(
    c(max(abs(F(lambda_hat))) / n1,
      mec$calibration$max_mean_balance_residual), scientific = TRUE, digits = 3
  )
), digits = 6,

The worked solver uses S2.4’s numerical choices. The package solves the same KL balance equation using a scaled ridge, a dual-objective line search, and calibration_tol applied to max⁡|F|/n1\max|F|/n_1 (default 10−810^{-8}). Accordingly, the comparison checks numerical agreement rather than identical iterations. The public fit_mec_cox() implementation uses KL calibration; the supplement’s general GG notation also describes other generators.

For routine analysis, the package also returns the MEC uncertainty estimates:

data.frame(hazard_ratio = mec$hr, SE_log_hazard_ratio = mec$se,
           CI_lower = unname(mec$conf_int["lower"]),
           CI_upper = unname(mec$conf_int["upper"]))
#>   hazard_ratio SE_log_hazard_ratio CI_lower CI_upper
#> 1      1.09407            0.135446 0.838986  1.42672

4-2. Comparison with standard ATT-IPW Cox methods

We now compare MEC-Cox with the three standard ATT-IPW Cox analyses described in the paper: naive, robust sandwich, and corrected sandwich. These three analyses share one set of baseline ATT weights and one weighted Cox point estimate. Their standard errors and confidence intervals differ because they use different variance estimators. MEC-Cox uses its calibrated weights and the stacked sandwich variance from the preceding implementation.

For the standard comparators, fit_att_ipw_cox() fits a logistic-regression source propensity model once to the full pooled sample. It converts the fitted probabilities to external-control odds and normalizes these weights to sum to n1n_1, using the same odds-and-normalization construction as Step 2. Treated subjects retain weight one. The call below uses the same subjects and baseline covariates as the worked MEC-Cox example.

  1. Naive: ATT-IPW Cox with naive model-based variance. This analysis uses the usual inverse-information variance from the weighted Cox partial likelihood, treating the estimated ATT weights as fixed. It adds neither a robust sandwich correction nor an estimating-equation block for the fitted propensity model. This corresponds to the model-based variance comparator discussed in the paper and by Austin (2016).

  2. Robust sandwich: ATT-IPW Cox with Lin–Wei/Binder robust variance. This analysis uses the same ATT-IPW coefficient as the naive analysis, but constructs its variance from the subject-level Cox contributions, including their effects through the weighted risk sets. It treats the fitted propensity-score weights as fixed. Consequently, it does not incorporate their estimation through the logistic score equation, and it can yield conservative inference. See Lin and Wei (1989), Binder (1992), and Shu et al. (2021).

  3. Corrected sandwich: ATT-IPW Cox with Shu corrected sandwich variance. This analysis retains the same ATT-IPW coefficient and stacks the weighted Cox estimating equation with the logistic source-propensity score equation. The cross-derivative accounts for the dependence of the normalized ATT weights on the fitted logistic coefficients. The package follows the paper’s joint Cox/logistic-score convention, based on Shu et al. (2021). Its validity relies on the corresponding propensity-model and regularity conditions; this correction does not repair misspecified propensity weights or directly extend the logistic score calculation to an arbitrary ML learner.

  4. MEC-Cox: calibrated weights with the proposed stacked sandwich variance. This analysis uses the cross-fitted source propensities and control-survival features from Steps 1–2, calibrates the external-control weights in Steps 3–5, and fits the final weighted Cox model in Step 6. Its variance stacks the Cox contribution with the calibration equations. The table reuses mec from Section 4-1, including the selected propensity learner, survival learner, and kl_derivative option.

The standard ATT-IPW comparators use the full-sample logistic fit, whereas MEC-Cox uses the selected cross-fitted propensity learner and subsequent calibration. The comparison therefore follows the paper’s complete methods: differences between the ATT-IPW and MEC-Cox point estimates reflect their weight construction, including propensity fitting and calibration. Changing ps_method in Step 2 changes the MEC-Cox row; the three standard comparator rows retain their logistic-regression specification.

att_ipw <- fit_att_ipw_cox(
  dat, time = "time", event = "event", source = "source",
  covariates = X_names, ps_clip = ps_trim,
  conf_level = mec$conf_level
)

variance_methods <- c("naive", "robust", "corrected")
att_intervals <- att_ipw$conf_int[
  match(variance_methods, att_ipw$conf_int$method), , drop = FALSE
]
stopifnot(identical(att_intervals$method, variance_methods))

method_comparison <- data.frame(
  Method = c("ATT-IPW: naive model-based",
             "ATT-IPW: Lin-Wei/Binder robust",
             "ATT-IPW: Shu corrected", "MEC-Cox"),
  Log_HR = c(rep(att_ipw$theta, 3L), mec$theta),
  HR = c(rep(att_ipw$hr, 3L), mec$hr),
  SE = c(unname(att_ipw$se[variance_methods]), mec$se),
  Lower = c(att_intervals$hazard_lower, unname(mec$conf_int["lower"])),
  Upper = c(att_intervals$hazard_upper, unname(mec$conf_int["upper"])),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(method_comparison, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Method", "Log HR", "HR", "SE (log HR)",
                           "CI lower", "CI upper"),
             caption = sprintf("Comparison using %g%% confidence intervals.",
                               100 * mec$conf_level))
Comparison using 95% confidence intervals.
Method Log HR HR SE (log HR) CI lower CI upper
ATT-IPW: naive model-based 0.0935 1.0980 0.1475 0.8224 1.4660
ATT-IPW: Lin-Wei/Binder robust 0.0935 1.0980 0.1493 0.8195 1.4711
ATT-IPW: Shu corrected 0.0935 1.0980 0.1416 0.8319 1.4493
MEC-Cox 0.0899 1.0941 0.1354 0.8390 1.4267

The first three rows have the same log hazard ratio and hazard ratio. Their different intervals arise entirely from their standard errors. All intervals are Wald intervals obtained on the log-hazard-ratio scale and then exponentiated. The MEC-Cox row can differ in both its point estimate and its standard error because it uses calibrated weights and a different stacked estimating system. A smaller reported standard error in this example is a comparison of estimated uncertainty for these data; bias and coverage require the repeated-sampling evaluations presented in the paper.

4-3. KL cross-derivative: numerical and analytic calculation

The kl_derivative option in fit_mec_cox() selects how one block of the stacked-sandwich Jacobian is evaluated. Its default is "numerical"; "analytic" uses the KL identity derived below. Both choices use the same estimated propensity scores, prognostic basis, calibrated weights, and Cox coefficient. The choice concerns the variance calculation after fitting. To select a method, change kl_derivative in the package call above and rerun from that chunk. The comparison below always evaluates both choices and identifies the selected one.

Write U(θ,λ)=UMEC,θ(θ,λ)U(\theta,\lambda)=U_{\mathrm{MEC},\theta}(\theta,\lambda) for the weighted Cox score from Step 6. The cross-derivative is the row vector

Dθλ(θ,λ)=∂U(θ,λ)∂λ⊤∈ℝ1×p. D_{\theta\lambda}(\theta,\lambda) =\frac{\partial U(\theta,\lambda)}{\partial\lambda^\top} \in\mathbb R^{1\times p}.

Here the nuisance predictions, d̂i\widehat d_i, ĥi\widehat h_i, and θ\theta are held fixed while λ\lambda varies. This differs from the calibration Jacobian J(λ)=∂F(λ)/∂λ⊤J(\lambda)=\partial F(\lambda)/\partial\lambda^\top used in Step 5: JJ differentiates the balance equations and is a p×pp\times p matrix; DθλD_{\theta\lambda} differentiates the Cox score and has one row.

The calculation below reuses the fitted mec object. It does not refit nuisance learners, calibration, or the Cox coefficient.

kl_derivative <- match.arg(kl_derivative, c("numerical", "analytic"))
fixed_data <- mec$analysis_data
fixed_theta <- mec$theta
fixed_lambda <- mec$calibration$lambda
fixed_omega <- mec$weights
fixed_H <- mec$basis
fixed_I0 <- which(fixed_data$A == 0L)
fixed_I1 <- which(fixed_data$A == 1L)
fixed_H0 <- fixed_H[fixed_I0, , drop = FALSE]
fixed_d <- mec$baseline_weights[fixed_I0]
fixed_p <- ncol(fixed_H)

omega_at_lambda <- function(candidate) {
  omega <- rep(1, nrow(fixed_data))
  omega[fixed_I0] <- fixed_d * exp(drop(fixed_H0 %*% candidate))
  omega
}
stopifnot(max(abs(omega_at_lambda(fixed_lambda) - fixed_omega)) < 1e-10)

For a fixed pair (θ,λ)(\theta,\lambda), abbreviate ω̃i=ω̃i(λ)\widetilde\omega_i=\widetilde\omega_i(\lambda) and A¯(t)=A¯MEC,ω̃(t;θ,λ)\overline A(t)=\overline A_{\mathrm{MEC},\widetilde\omega}(t;\theta,\lambda). To make the risk-set calculation explicit, let ℰ(t)\mathcal E(t) be the subjects with an observed event at tt, and ℛ(t)\mathcal R(t) those still at risk, including subjects whose observed follow-up ends at tt. Define

mω(t)=∑i∈ℰ(t)ω̃i,Sλ(r)(t;θ)=∑i∈ℛ(t)ω̃ieθAiAir,A¯(t)=Sλ(1)(t;θ)Sλ(0)(t;θ). m_\omega(t)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal E(t)}\widetilde\omega_i, \qquad S^{(r)}_\lambda(t;\theta)= \sum_{i\in\mathcal R(t)}\widetilde\omega_i e^{\theta A_i}A_i^r, \qquad \overline A(t)=\frac{S^{(1)}_\lambda(t;\theta)} {S^{(0)}_\lambda(t;\theta)}.

The following function evaluates the score using Breslow handling of tied events. It also evaluates the complete Lin–Wei/Binder empirical contribution ηi\eta_i from Supplement S2.5. This contribution includes both a subject’s event and its effect on every weighted risk set in which it appears:

ηi(θ,λ)=∫ω̃i(λ){Ai−A¯(t)}d𝒩i(t)−∫ω̃i(λ)𝒴i(t)eθAi{Ai−A¯(t)}Sλ(0)(t;θ)d𝒩ω,λ(t), \eta_i(\theta,\lambda) =\int \widetilde\omega_i(\lambda) \{A_i-\overline A(t)\}\,d\mathcal N_i(t) -\int\frac{\widetilde\omega_i(\lambda)\mathcal Y_i(t)e^{\theta A_i} \{A_i-\overline A(t)\}} {S^{(0)}_\lambda(t;\theta)} \,d\mathcal N_{\omega,\lambda}(t),

where d𝒩ω,λ(t)=∑jω̃j(λ)d𝒩j(t)d\mathcal N_{\omega,\lambda}(t)= \sum_j\widetilde\omega_j(\lambda)\,d\mathcal N_j(t).

weighted_cox_components <- function(theta, analysis_data, omega) {
  A <- analysis_data$A
  time <- analysis_data$time
  event <- analysis_data$delta
  event_times <- sort(unique(time[event == 1L]))
  score <- 0
  eta <- numeric(length(A))
  for (t in event_times) {
    events <- which(time == t & event == 1L)
    risk <- which(time >= t)
    risk_weight <- omega[risk] * exp(theta * A[risk])
    S0 <- sum(risk_weight)
    Abar <- sum(risk_weight * A[risk]) / S0
    event_mass <- sum(omega[events])
    event_part <- omega[events] * (A[events] - Abar)
    score <- score + sum(event_part)
    eta[events] <- eta[events] + event_part
    eta[risk] <- eta[risk] - risk_weight * event_mass / S0 *
      (A[risk] - Abar)
  }
  list(score = score, eta = eta)
}

fixed_cox <- weighted_cox_components(fixed_theta, fixed_data, fixed_omega)
stopifnot(abs(sum(fixed_cox$eta) - fixed_cox$score) < 1e-10)

Numerical calculation. For component jj, use the central difference

D̂θλ,jnum=U(θ̂MEC,λ̂+ϵjej)−U(θ̂MEC,λ̂−ϵjej)2ϵj,ϵj=10−5max⁡(1,|λ̂j|), \widehat D_{\theta\lambda,j}^{\mathrm{num}} =\frac{U(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MEC}}, \widehat\lambda+\epsilon_j e_j) -U(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MEC}}, \widehat\lambda-\epsilon_j e_j)}{2\epsilon_j}, \qquad \epsilon_j=10^{-5}\max(1,|\widehat\lambda_j|),

where eje_j is the jjth coordinate vector. Each perturbation changes the external-control weights and therefore both the event terms and risk-set averages. Perturbed weights are not renormalized or recalibrated, and θ\theta is not re-estimated: those operations would differentiate a different map.

central_difference <- function(fun, x) {
  derivative <- numeric(length(x))
  for (j in seq_along(x)) {
    increment <- 1e-5 * max(1, abs(x[j]))
    plus <- minus <- x
    plus[j] <- plus[j] + increment
    minus[j] <- minus[j] - increment
    derivative[j] <- (fun(plus) - fun(minus)) / (2 * increment)
  }
  derivative
}
score_at_lambda <- function(candidate) {
  weighted_cox_components(fixed_theta, fixed_data,
                          omega_at_lambda(candidate))$score
}
derivative_numerical <- central_difference(score_at_lambda, fixed_lambda)

Analytic calculation for KL. Since wi(λ)=d̂iexp⁡(λ⊤ĥi)w_i(\lambda)=\widehat d_i\exp(\lambda^\top\widehat h_i),

∂wi(λ)∂λj=wi(λ)ĥij,i∈ℐ0, \frac{\partial w_i(\lambda)}{\partial\lambda_j} =w_i(\lambda)\widehat h_{ij},\qquad i\in\mathcal I_0,

and treated subjects have derivative zero. Differentiating the score’s event weights and risk-set averages gives

∂U∂λj=∑i∈ℐ0ĥij[∫wi{Ai−A¯(t)}d𝒩i(t)−∫wi𝒴i(t)eθAi{Ai−A¯(t)}Sλ(0)(t;θ)d𝒩ω,λ(t)]. \frac{\partial U}{\partial\lambda_j} =\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0}\widehat h_{ij} \left[ \int w_i\{A_i-\overline A(t)\}\,d\mathcal N_i(t) -\int\frac{w_i\mathcal Y_i(t)e^{\theta A_i} \{A_i-\overline A(t)\}} {S^{(0)}_\lambda(t;\theta)} \,d\mathcal N_{\omega,\lambda}(t) \right].

The bracket is exactly ηi(θ,λ)\eta_i(\theta,\lambda). At the fitted pair, η̂i=ηi(θ̂MEC,λ̂)\widehat\eta_i=\eta_i(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MEC}},\widehat\lambda), so

D̂θλana=∑i∈ℐ0η̂iĥi⊤. \widehat D_{\theta\lambda}^{\mathrm{ana}} =\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0}\widehat\eta_i \widehat h_i^\top.

Using only the direct event contribution would omit the derivative of the risk-set average. The full eta vector above supplies both terms.

derivative_analytic <- drop(crossprod(fixed_cox$eta[fixed_I0], fixed_H0))
feature_names <- c("Intercept", paste0("S0(t=", mec$landmark_times, ")"))[
  mec$retained_basis
]
derivative_comparison <- data.frame(
  Feature = feature_names,
  Numerical = derivative_numerical,
  Analytic = derivative_analytic,
  Absolute_difference = abs(derivative_numerical - derivative_analytic)
)
knitr::kable(derivative_comparison, digits = c(0, 8, 8, 12), row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Feature", "Numerical", "Analytic", "Absolute difference"))
Feature Numerical Analytic Absolute difference
Intercept 0.067066 0.067066 1.20e-11
S0(t=3) 1.318324 1.318324 3.14e-10

Effect on the stacked-sandwich calculation. Define the calibration contribution for each subject as

ρ̂i={ŵiĥi,i∈ℐ0,−ĥi,i∈ℐ1,Ψ̂i=(η̂iρ̂i). \widehat\rho_i=\begin{cases} \widehat w_i\widehat h_i,&i\in\mathcal I_0,\\ -\widehat h_i,&i\in\mathcal I_1, \end{cases} \qquad \widehat\Psi_i=\begin{pmatrix}\widehat\eta_i\\\widehat\rho_i\end{pmatrix}.

Let â\widehat a be ∂U/∂θ\partial U/\partial\theta evaluated at (θ̂MEC,λ̂)(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MEC}},\widehat\lambda). Using the calibration Jacobian from Step 5, the full Jacobian is

D̂stack=(âD̂θλ0J(λ̂)). \widehat D_{\mathrm{stack}} =\begin{pmatrix}\widehat a&\widehat D_{\theta\lambda}\\0&J(\widehat\lambda)\end{pmatrix}.

When this matrix is nonsingular, the sandwich covariance is

V̂=D̂stack−1(∑i=1nΨ̂iΨ̂i⊤)D̂stack−⊤. \widehat V =\widehat D_{\mathrm{stack}}^{-1} \left(\sum_{i=1}^n\widehat\Psi_i\widehat\Psi_i^\top\right) \widehat D_{\mathrm{stack}}^{-\top}.

These use summed equations and summed subject contributions, so there is no additional 1/n1/n factor. The estimated standard error of the log hazard ratio is V̂11\sqrt{\widehat V_{11}}. Both choices below retain the package’s numerical calculation of â\widehat a and its singular-value cutoff; only D̂θλ\widehat D_{\theta\lambda} changes. If the cutoff removes a direction, the code uses the same generalized inverse as the package in place of the ordinary inverse.

a_theta <- central_difference(function(candidate) {
  weighted_cox_components(candidate[1L], fixed_data, fixed_omega)$score
}, fixed_theta)
J_fixed <- crossprod(fixed_H0 * fixed_omega[fixed_I0], fixed_H0)
calibration_rows <- matrix(0, nrow(fixed_data), fixed_p)
calibration_rows[fixed_I0, ] <- fixed_H0 * fixed_omega[fixed_I0]
calibration_rows[fixed_I1, ] <- -fixed_H[fixed_I1, , drop = FALSE]
psi_rows <- cbind(fixed_cox$eta, calibration_rows)

sandwich_with_cross_derivative <- function(derivative_lambda) {
  D_stack <- rbind(c(a_theta, derivative_lambda), cbind(rep(0, fixed_p), J_fixed))
  decomposition <- svd(D_stack)
  retain <- decomposition$d > max(decomposition$d) * 1e-8
  stopifnot(any(retain))
  D_inverse <- decomposition$v[, retain, drop = FALSE] %*%
    (t(decomposition$u[, retain, drop = FALSE]) / decomposition$d[retain])
  influence_theta <- -drop(psi_rows %*% D_inverse[1L, ])
  se <- sqrt(sum(influence_theta^2))
  critical_value <- qnorm((1 + mec$conf_level) / 2)
  interval <- exp(fixed_theta + c(-1, 1) * critical_value * se)
  list(se = se, interval = interval, rank = sum(retain),
       used_pseudoinverse = !all(retain), influence = influence_theta)
}
kl_results <- list(
  numerical = sandwich_with_cross_derivative(derivative_numerical),
  analytic = sandwich_with_cross_derivative(derivative_analytic)
)
uncertainty_comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(kl_results), function(choice) {
  result <- kl_results[[choice]]
  data.frame(Derivative = choice, Selected = choice == kl_derivative,
             HR = exp(fixed_theta),
             SE_log_HR = result$se,
             CI_lower = result$interval[1L], CI_upper = result$interval[2L])
}))
knitr::kable(uncertainty_comparison, digits = 9,
  col.names = c("Derivative", "Selected", "HR", "SE (log HR)",
                "CI lower", "CI upper"))
Derivative Selected HR SE (log HR) CI lower CI upper
numerical TRUE 1.09407 0.135446 0.838986 1.42672
analytic FALSE 1.09407 0.135446 0.838986 1.42672 
# This is the same selection passed to fit_mec_cox() above.
selected_kl_result <- kl_results[[kl_derivative]]
stopifnot(
  max(abs(derivative_numerical - derivative_analytic)) < 1e-5 * max(1, max(abs(derivative_analytic))),
  abs(selected_kl_result$se - mec$se) < 1e-7
)

The Selected column identifies the option passed to the package call above. The common HR in the table is expected: the two calculations reuse exactly the same fitted coefficient. Any difference in SE or confidence limits here comes from numerical approximation of the cross-derivative. The analytic identity uses the KL exponential weight map; it does not by itself provide the corresponding formula for a different Bregman generator.

4-4. Run or rebuild this manual

Download the R Markdown source and run its chunks in order in RStudio, or use Knit to recreate this HTML page.
